Guptas' Dominion

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Yet another Gupta family scam -- the uranium mine bought with R1bn taxpayers' and several banks' money is worth almost nothing, as uranium cannot be profitably mined there

Summary:
The Dominion uranium deposit on the Afrikander Lease site south of Klerksdorp was discovered in the 1940s when atom bomb builders considered the deposit for supplying the Manhattan project -- it was determined then already that the uranium, although possibly the largest deposit in the world, was not of sufficient quality to be mined profitably. It was abandoned at that stage.
In 1996 the new owners of the property, Anglo American conducted a R120-million geological study to see if the uranium could be productively mined. They determined the quality was not sufficient.
In 1997 mining engineer Peter Skeat bought Afrikander Leases from Anglo and even he conducted the experiments and surveys to determine how he could profitably mine the uranium. While in this position, Skeat won the Department of Trade and Industry's TOP 300 companies award and twice, the JSE's top gold share award. Skeat's research basically confirmed the findings by Anglo American.
Skeat was swindled out of his company by Brett Kebble and his collaborators (Skeat was vindicated after 6-year long court case and got about R40-m back after the court found in his favour agains Kebble & co.)
Skeat's successor was Neal Froneman, who incurred a $1.8-billion loss at the Afrikaner Lease/Dominion property -- the history is well documented.
Now Oakbay Resources acquired the Uranium Mine, using R1-bn of tax-payers' money, and a number of banks have contributed.
We investigate who stands to lose how much now that the family seems to have abandoned their directorships and the mirage of Oakbay's market capitalisation, based on a share price that is manipulated and meaningless is exposed.
The Guptas never paid for what is now named Shiva. The deposit is worthless, and will take billions to recapitalise if it is to ever go into commercial production. Even at current rand/dollar rate, it would require the price of uranium oxide to be four times higher than prevailing US$ world price.

Press Release:


GUPTA PROMOS


TEN
Has the Gupta’s Uranium discovered the secret to tapping the riches of a uranium mine that’s never turned a profit? Or is this a bid to own our nuclear energy future?

FIFTEEN
VO: The Gupta mine at Dominion Reef has never been mined profitably for uranium so why did the IDC fund it?
BARRY SERGEANT: It doesn’t really matter what the Guptas do or don’t do, they’re just part of an ongoing fairy story about Dominion and now Shiva.

FIFTEEN
PETER SKEAT: It’s not worth any more than the grazing rights for the cattle that graze the grass for the extent of the deposit…
VO: Did taxpayers fork out quarter of a billion rand on a uranium mine for the Gupta’s that is unlikely to turn a profit?


Script:


GUPTA URANIUM SCRIPT
Dominion Reef, outside Klerkdorp in the NorthWest Province. Its enormous uranium deposits promise a holy grail of mining riches. But as one company after another has discovered since the mid-1900s, the mine’s promise is an empty one.
Dominion’s uranium deposits have never been mined profitably – and nearby Dominionville remains a ghost town.
Today, Shiva Uranium, owned by the billionaire Gupta family – whose alleged capture of the South African state regularly dominates headlines – is the latest owner to promise great returns from Dominion Reef.
GEOFFREY QHENA, CEO, IDC: When project was up and running there would be 4500 jobs which would have been created. That’s one of the attractions.
PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: Isn’t it worth to give this mine a chance…it was employing 3000 people, even if we can make it run half its planned rate, there’s 1500 jobs we’ve created, we’ve prevented a town from going broke.
A quarter of a billion rands in taxpayers’ money was invested in Oakbay Resources and Energy, which listed on the JSE in 2014, so have they discovered the secret to tapping Dominion’s uranium riches? Or is this a bid to own South Africa’s nuclear energy future?
Understanding the story of Dominion hinges on the fact that in the last 30 years the price of uranium has not averaged above $40 per pound until a three-year spike form 2004.
PETER MAJOR: The uranium price went from $7 to 20, 40 to 60, before you knew it, it was $140 a pound, so you could almost mine Table Mountain for uranium and make money at $140 per pound.
Financial author Barry Sergeant has tracked the story of Dominion from the nineties.
BARRY SERGEANT: There are certain sections where the gold is quite rich and that’s where Peter Skeat was mining.
Mining engineer Peter Skeat bought Dominion from Anglo American in ‘97. Skeat, like Anglo before him, worked the small gold deposit.
BARRY SERGEANT: Somebody like Peter Skeat who’s a specialist, he could turn it into a tiny operation and make some money out of it – one or two million rand a month. So that, in South African terms, is a tiny gold mine.
Skeat won awards for the best gold share on the Stock Exchange, but no matter how he tested the soil and scoured half a century’s geological surveys, he was unable to mine the uranium deposit profitably.
PETER SKEAT: It starts really in World War II when the Americans were building an atom bomb for the Pacific war and they needed supplies of uranium and they’d sent exploration teams to the Congo and to Namibia and they sent one to Dominion and they came to the conclusion that very exciting deposit, enormous, but not viable…Anglo bought it in the 1980s and they spent hundreds of millions of rands exploring the area and they produced what is known as the Dominion bible… Anglo’s conclusion after their investigation was wonderful deposit, but the production cost is too high.
BONGANI BINGWA: Why is it too expensive?
PETER SKEAT: The grade is low…all these reefs are underwater, so you’ve got a huge pumping problem.
Skeat’s run the numbers repeatedly. Dominion can only work with another miraculous uranium price spike.
PETER SKEAT: The average price for uranium at the moment is 28 dollars per pound…you can buy it anywhere else in the world for a fifth of what Dominion will produce it...it’s not worth any more than the grazing rights for the cattle.
Dominion seized the imagination of mining magnate Brett Kebble who – as history shows – had captured sections of the governing party through financial favours. With associates Kebble hatched a plan to hijack Skeat’s mine. They concocted fraud charges against him and Skeat had to resign.
BONGANI BINGWA: What did they accuse you of?
PETER SKEAT: All sorts of weird charges – they said I had flown to the Congo, bought gold …and sprinkled the gold over the open cast pit to supposedly increase the grades so that our results looked good...now I have to go to court and explain this ridiculous story…we won on every single count plus interests plus costs…but it took a period of 3 or 4 years.
When armed thugs attacked his house, the corporate battle almost cost Skeat his life.
Dominion’s fate shifted again when Kebble was killed in 2005 – new owners Uranium1 set about marketing the vast resource and raised billions for a shiny hi-tech processing plant. But it failed.
BARRY SERGEANT: Going into 2008 you could see that the plant was going to die, and it did. And there was an impairment raised in the books after the closure in 2008 – 1,8 billion US dollars. And as far as I know it’s the biggest write-off in South African history.
Enter the Guptas, who started negotiating in 2008 to buy Dominion and the R4-billion plant, now for sale at the bargain price of R250-million. Investment analyst Peter Major was one of many specialists working on the deal.
PETER MAJOR: The owners, Uranium1 had very rich operating uranium mines in Kazakhstan that could make money at $20 a pound, so it just wanted to dispose of this and it looked like this asset could be acquired for $40 million.
By the time the Guptas owned Dominion in 2010, the uranium boom had ended. But despite this, and the mine’s history the Industrial Development Corporation was persuaded to provide the substantial R250-million loan with which Oakbay Resources bought Dominion.
BONGANI LINK: Extensive reports and the experience of no less a corporate giant than Anglo American showed that the Gupta’s Klerksdorp mine cannot be mined profitably – so why did the IDC take a bet on it?
CEO Geoffrey Qhena is mandated to finance promising enterprises that will mobilize the South African economy, using taxpayers’ money. And in 2008, plans for new nuclear power generation were firmly on the table, ere and abroad.
BONGANI BINGWA: I have a graph here that tracks what the price of uranium had been since 1986 – by the time you do the deal there was a brief spike…in the previous 30 years, the uranium price had always averaged under $40 – what made you think it was going to go and stay around 60?
GEOFFREY QHENA: We looked at the number of new power plants that were going to come in that were going to be nuclear…if you look in Asia, there’s still lots of opportunities – if we are going to industrialise, we need to look at all sources of energy.
BONGANI BINGWA: If you are anticipating a government nuclear build program is this the kind of thing you get involved in?
PETER MAJOR: That would be a good angle it’s a good way of playing it. If this country is looking at building a lot of nuclear reactors and we think the uranium price is going to be $60 we are going to be large producer again and this company would have been leading the charge.
BONGANI BINGWA: Did the promises of this opportunity materialize?
GEOFFREY QHENA: When we got involved into the transaction the uranium price was about $60 per pound…you will recall there was a tsunami in Japan and Fukushima – and the uranium price dropped to about $40 per pound 8 months later…what then they did was to continue to process the gold …which is why the 4500 jobs we anticipated were not there.
Oakbay told us in writing that the mine employs “around 800 people”; they’re keeping the plant in regular care and maintenance; they’re mining and processing the gold…but what about financial returns? Oakbay Resources was late paying back the loan by 2013. The IDC was nice enough to reschedule their debt – by taking a tiny 3,57% share in the company when it listed on the JSE in 2014.
R117-million of the original loan remains outstanding.
BONGANI BINGWA: Why did you not foreclose at that stage?
GEOFFREY QHENA: As I said we take a long-term view – it’s not unusual, there’s a lot of those clients that – I always say to our guys, we always give an opportunity.
PETER MAJOR: That plant is still in very good shape it’s a beautiful plant, those autoclaves can be used on a goldmine, so can the IDC get their money out of this – I think if they drove into Dominion and they had the sheriff with them and I gave him permission I think I could probably recover most of their money.
BONGANI LINK: Being a JSE listed company comes with a lot of prestige – from a reputational point of view it suggests you’re in the big leagues…but does it mean that everything is above board?
PETER MAJOR: We are not sure what the value of Oakbay is based on. It seems to have an incredibly high price.
BARRY SERGEANT: Not many shares are freely floating and if some shares do come onto the market the owners… tend to have stock brokers watching for shares that come into the market in that company, for example Oakbay, and they are instructed to buy them up, to mop them up. And that way the price is manipulated, not in a criminal way, but in a very uncivil way.
Oakbay told us they put the value of their gold, uranium and some coal assets at a “combined R10.8-billion”; they’re “up to date” with IDC repayments and “majority of market analysts expect an upswing in uranium prices”. They insist their “bankable feasibility study showed Dominion Reef is viable for mining uranium”. But tell that to the community on the ground.
BONGANI LINK: You would think that a mining town sitting on top of a significant mineral resource deposit would be booming and thriving…well, the community is nearly deserted. We’re told that even the local shop only opens once a month when there are social grants to be made.
For locals like Advocate Nkewana questions linger about how taxpayers’ money has brought so little return.
ADVOCATE NKEWANA: We are having many mines around this area, even if we have to leave now and wait for two hours, we won’t see even one truck there. The next thing you will see is police they will come and ask you why are you parking there.
BONGANI BINGWA: What’s your response to the allegation, or suggestion that pressure was brought to bear on the IDC to fund this, to restructure it, no matter what?
GEOFFREY QHENA: We have here a concentrate of lawyers, accountants, engineers and we had those people who did the due diligence…so at no point – I’ve asked the team – when this hit the newspapers, I asked my team, “was any of you asked to do this transaction at all costs? And I got an answer, “no”.
BONGANI BINGWA: What will it take for you to realise you did your best, this is not going to be viable?
GEOFFREY QHENA: Obviously I think what we see now, presently, which is worrisome…all the four major banks have decided not to support this, so one needs to see what the solution is…at least, the next instalment is due by the end of June…so we will see.

But as one company after another has discovered since the mid-1900s, the mine’s promise is an empty one. Dominion’s uranium deposits have never been mined profitably – and nearby Dominionville remains a ghost town. Today, Shiva Uranium, owned by the billionaire Gupta family – whose alleged capture of the South African state regularly dominates headlines – is the latest owner to promise great returns from Dominion Reef. GEOFFREY QHENA, CEO, IDC: When project was up and running there would be 4500 jobs which would have been created. That’s one of the attractions. PETER MAJOR, DIRECTOR MINING, CADIZ CORPORATE SOLUTIONS: Isn’t it worth to give this mine a chance…it was employing 3000 people, even if we can make it run half its planned rate, there’s 1500 jobs we’ve created, we’ve prevented a town from going broke. A quarter of a billion rands in taxpayers’ money was invested in Oakbay Resources and Energy, which listed on the JSE in 2014, so have they discovered the secret to tapping Dominion’s uranium riches? Or is this a bid to own South Africa’s nuclear energy future? Understanding the story of Dominion hinges on the fact that in the last 30 years the price of uranium has not averaged above $40 per pound until a three-year spike form 2004. PETER MAJOR: The uranium price went from $7 to 20, 40 to 60, before you knew it, it was $140 a pound, so you could almost mine Table Mountain for uranium and make money at $140 per pound. Financial author Barry Sergeant has tracked the story of Dominion from the nineties. BARRY SERGEANT: There are certain sections where the gold is quite rich and that’s where Peter Skeat was mining. Mining engineer Peter Skeat bought Dominion from Anglo American in ‘97. Skeat, like Anglo before him, worked the small gold deposit. BARRY SERGEANT: Somebody like Peter Skeat who’s a specialist, he could turn it into a tiny operation and make some money out of it – one or two million rand a month. So that, in South African terms, is a tiny gold mine. Skeat won awards for the best gold share on the Stock Exchange, but no matter how he tested the soil and scoured half a century’s geological surveys, he was unable to mine the uranium deposit profitably. PETER SKEAT: It starts really in World War II when the Americans were building an atom bomb for the Pacific war and they needed supplies of uranium and they’d sent exploration teams to the Congo and to Namibia and they sent one to Dominion and they came to the conclusion that very exciting deposit, enormous, but not viable…Anglo bought it in the 1980s and they spent hundreds of millions of rands exploring the area and they produced what is known as the Dominion bible… Anglo’s conclusion after their investigation was wonderful deposit, but the production cost is too high. BONGANI BINGWA: Why is it too expensive? PETER SKEAT: The grade is low…all these reefs are underwater, so you’ve got a huge pumping problem. Skeat’s run the numbers repeatedly. Dominion can only work with another miraculous uranium price spike. PETER SKEAT: The average price for uranium at the moment is 28 dollars per pound…you can buy it anywhere else in the world for a fifth of what Dominion will produce it...it’s not worth any more than the grazing rights for the cattle. Dominion seized the imagination of mining magnate Brett Kebble who – as history shows – had captured sections of the governing party through financial favours. With associates Kebble hatched a plan to hijack Skeat’s mine. They concocted fraud charges against him and Skeat had to resign. BONGANI BINGWA: What did they accuse you of? PETER SKEAT: All sorts of weird charges – they said I had flown to the Congo, bought gold …and sprinkled the gold over the open cast pit to supposedly increase the grades so that our results looked good...now I have to go to court and explain this ridiculous story…we won on every single count plus interests plus costs…but it took a period of 3 or 4 years. When armed thugs attacked his house, the corporate battle almost cost Skeat his life. Dominion’s fate shifted again when Kebble was killed in 2005 – new owners Uranium1 set about marketing the vast resource and raised billions for a shiny hi-tech processing plant. But it failed. BARRY SERGEANT: Going into 2008 you could see that the plant was going to die, and it did. And there was an impairment raised in the books after the closure in 2008 – 1,8 billion US dollars. And as far as I know it’s the biggest write-off in South African history. Enter the Guptas, who started negotiating in 2008 to buy Dominion and the R4-billion plant, now for sale at the bargain price of R250-million. Investment analyst Peter Major was one of many specialists working on the deal. PETER MAJOR: The owners, Uranium1 had very rich operating uranium mines in Kazakhstan that could make money at $20 a pound, so it just wanted to dispose of this and it looked like this asset could be acquired for $40 million. By the time the Guptas owned Dominion in 2010, the uranium boom had ended. But despite this, and the mine’s history the Industrial Development Corporation was persuaded to provide the substantial R250-million loan with which Oakbay Resources bought Dominion. BONGANI LINK: Extensive reports and the experience of no less a corporate giant than Anglo American showed that the Gupta’s Klerksdorp mine cannot be mined profitably – so why did the IDC take a bet on it? CEO Geoffrey Qhena is mandated to finance promising enterprises that will mobilize the South African economy, using taxpayers’ money. And in 2008, plans for new nuclear power generation were firmly on the table, ere and abroad. BONGANI BINGWA: I have a graph here that tracks what the price of uranium had been since 1986 – by the time you do the deal there was a brief spike…in the previous 30 years, the uranium price had always averaged under $40 – what made you think it was going to go and stay around 60? GEOFFREY QHENA: We looked at the number of new power plants that were going to come in that were going to be nuclear…if you look in Asia, there’s still lots of opportunities – if we are going to industrialise, we need to look at all sources of energy. BONGANI BINGWA: If you are anticipating a government nuclear build program is this the kind of thing you get involved in? PETER MAJOR: That would be a good angle it’s a good way of playing it. If this country is looking at building a lot of nuclear reactors and we think the uranium price is going to be $60 we are going to be large producer again and this company would have been leading the charge. BONGANI BINGWA: Did the promises of this opportunity materialize? GEOFFREY QHENA: When we got involved into the transaction the uranium price was about $60 per pound…you will recall there was a tsunami in Japan and Fukushima – and the uranium price dropped to about $40 per pound 8 months later…what then they did was to continue to process the gold …which is why the 4500 jobs we anticipated were not there. Oakbay told us in writing that the mine employs “around 800 people”; they’re keeping the plant in regular care and maintenance; they’re mining and processing the gold…but what about financial returns? Oakbay Resources was late paying back the loan by 2013. The IDC was nice enough to reschedule their debt – by taking a tiny 3,57% share in the company when it listed on the JSE in 2014. R117-million of the original loan remains outstanding. BONGANI BINGWA: Why did you not foreclose at that stage? GEOFFREY QHENA: As I said we take a long-term view – it’s not unusual, there’s a lot of those clients that – I always say to our guys, we always give an opportunity. PETER MAJOR: That plant is still in very good shape it’s a beautiful plant, those autoclaves can be used on a goldmine, so can the IDC get their money out of this – I think if they drove into Dominion and they had the sheriff with them and I gave him permission I think I could probably recover most of their money. BONGANI LINK: Being a JSE listed company comes with a lot of prestige – from a reputational point of view it suggests you’re in the big leagues…but does it mean that everything is above board? PETER MAJOR: We are not sure what the value of Oakbay is based on. It seems to have an incredibly high price. BARRY SERGEANT: Not many shares are freely floating and if some shares do come onto the market the owners… tend to have stock brokers watching for shares that come into the market in that company, for example Oakbay, and they are instructed to buy them up, to mop them up. And that way the price is manipulated, not in a criminal way, but in a very uncivil way. Oakbay told us they put the value of their gold, uranium and some coal assets at a “combined R10.8-billion”; they’re “up to date” with IDC repayments and “majority of market analysts expect an upswing in uranium prices”. They insist their “bankable feasibility study showed Dominion Reef is viable for mining uranium”. But tell that to the community on the ground. BONGANI LINK: You would think that a mining town sitting on top of a significant mineral resource deposit would be booming and thriving…well, the community is nearly deserted. We’re told that even the local shop only opens once a month when there are social grants to be made. For locals like Advocate Nkewana questions linger about how taxpayers’ money has brought so little return. ADVOCATE NKEWANA: We are having many mines around this area, even if we have to leave now and wait for two hours, we won’t see even one truck there. The next thing you will see is police they will come and ask you why are you parking there. BONGANI BINGWA: What’s your response to the allegation, or suggestion that pressure was brought to bear on the IDC to fund this, to restructure it, no matter what? GEOFFREY QHENA: We have here a concentrate of lawyers, accountants, engineers and we had those people who did the due diligence…so at no point – I’ve asked the team – when this hit the newspapers, I asked my team, “was any of you asked to do this transaction at all costs? And I got an answer, “no”. BONGANI BINGWA: What will it take for you to realise you did your best, this is not going to be viable? GEOFFREY QHENA: Obviously I think what we see now, presently, which is worrisome…all the four major banks have decided not to support this, so one needs to see what the solution is…at least, the next instalment is due by the end of June…so we will see.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Yet another Gupta family scam -- the uranium mine bought with R1bn taxpayers' and several banks' money is worth almost nothing, as uranium cannot be profitably mined there
metadata.Summary: The Dominion uranium deposit on the Afrikander Lease site south of Klerksdorp was discovered in the 1940s when atom bomb builders considered the deposit for supplying the Manhattan project -- it was determined then already that the uranium, although possibly the largest deposit in the world, was not of sufficient quality to be mined profitably. It was abandoned at that stage. In 1996 the new owners of the property, Anglo American conducted a R120-million geological study to see if the uranium could be productively mined. They determined the quality was not sufficient. In 1997 mining engineer Peter Skeat bought Afrikander Leases from Anglo and even he conducted the experiments and surveys to determine how he could profitably mine the uranium. While in this position, Skeat won the Department of Trade and Industry's TOP 300 companies award and twice, the JSE's top gold share award. Skeat's research basically confirmed the findings by Anglo American. Skeat was swindled out of his company by Brett Kebble and his collaborators (Skeat was vindicated after 6-year long court case and got about R40-m back after the court found in his favour agains Kebble & co.) Skeat's successor was Neal Froneman, who incurred a $1.8-billion loss at the Afrikaner Lease/Dominion property -- the history is well documented. Now Oakbay Resources acquired the Uranium Mine, using R1-bn of tax-payers' money, and a number of banks have contributed. We investigate who stands to lose how much now that the family seems to have abandoned their directorships and the mirage of Oakbay's market capitalisation, based on a share price that is manipulated and meaningless is exposed. The Guptas never paid for what is now named Shiva. The deposit is worthless, and will take billions to recapitalise if it is to ever go into commercial production. Even at current rand/dollar rate, it would require the price of uranium oxide to be four times higher than prevailing US$ world price.
